analysis.one_liner: Bans corporations and investment funds from newly buying American farmland.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate on April 27, 2026 and referred to the Agriculture Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The Farmland for Farmers Act would make it illegal for most corporations and investment vehicles — including pension funds, mutual funds, and real estate investment trusts — to acquire or hold agricultural land, with exemptions only for genuine farmer cooperatives, small entities whose owners actively farm the land themselves, and a short list of exceptions like lenders selling off repossessed land. It would enforce this through annual sworn affidavits, loss of eligibility for USDA programs and Farm Credit System loans, civil penalties up to twice the land's value, forced divestiture ordered by federal courts, and criminal penalties of up to 5 years for individuals who knowingly violate it. The bill was introduced by Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ) and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, where it has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers and aspiring farmers who buy farmland would face less competition from deep-pocketed institutional investors that bid up land prices, and rural communities could see more land held by owner-operators with a long-term stake in it. Farmers using USDA programs and Farm Credit loans would also gain, because the bill disqualifies violating entities from those programs.

how_it_helps.text: It would bar new purchases of farmland by corporations, pension funds, investment funds, and other large entities, keeping land available for family farmers who would otherwise be outbid.
It defines allowed farm entities narrowly — no more than 25 natural-person owners, each actively working or managing the farm — so corporate holding structures cannot be used to evade the ban.
It lets state attorneys general sue violators on behalf of their residents and lets states adopt even stricter rules, giving local communities enforcement tools.

It exempts legitimate cases: cooperatives, nonprofits, research institutions, municipalities, heirs' property owners, lenders who acquire land through debt collection (if sold within 5 years), and entities that already owned farmland before enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, pension funds, and investment funds would be barred from a growing asset class they have increasingly bought since the 2008 financial crisis, and large existing farm entities would lose USDA program eligibility if they are structured outside the bill's exemptions. Landowners selling to corporate buyers could get somewhat lower prices.

drawbacks.text: The definition of an allowed 'authorized legal entity' is strict: no more than 25 owners, all of whom must be natural persons actively engaged in farming, and no layered holding-company structures, which could complicate legitimate family partnerships and multi-generation succession arrangements.

Enforcement is severe: violators face forced divestiture of land within one year, civil penalties up to twice the land's fair market value per violation, and up to 5 years in prison for individuals who knowingly violate the ban.

Entities already owning farmland are grandfathered, so the bill does not reduce existing corporate holdings — it only prevents new acquisitions, limiting how much it would change the current concentration of ownership.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real: farmland prices have roughly doubled since 2005, and institutional buyers price family farmers out of the market. The strongest honest objection is design risk: the definitions are blunt (capping ownership at 25 actively farming natural persons and barring layered entities), which could complicate legitimate partnerships, family succession planning through trusts, and some farm financing structures, and the enforcement machinery is severe (divestiture, criminal exposure). A weaker, better-tailored version could get the same anti-speculation result with less collateral damage.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee when introduced in April 2026 and has sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote since.

narrative.text: Introduced April 27, 2026 by Sen. Booker with Sen. Sanders; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day.
The bill has no further recorded action since that referral: no committee hearing, markup, or vote is listed in its action history.
Its only cosponsor is one of the Senate's two independents, and no Republican or additional Democratic cosponsors have joined.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Institutional investors and large corporate interests retain the ability to buy farmland and continue outbidding family farmers, which is the situation the bill was written to change.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Agriculture Committee.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's other original sponsor at introduction.

for.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
for.what_they_did: Holds the bill; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled for it.

sides.party_line_note: Both original sponsors are progressive, its one cosponsor is an independent, and no Republican has signed on, but no party bloc has taken any position because no vote has occurred.

industries.industry: Institutional investors in farmland (pension funds, mutual funds, REITs, investment companies)
industries.note: The bill bans them and similar investment vehicles from newly acquiring farmland and could impose penalties up to twice the land's value plus forced divestiture. Their loss would be prospective buyers' gain.

industries.industry: Large corporate farm operators and agribusiness holding companies
industries.note: Multi-layered corporate farm structures could no longer expand by buying land, and existing entities would lose eligibility for USDA programs and Farm Credit System lending.

industries.industry: Independent family farmers and farmer cooperatives
industries.note: Removing well-capitalized institutional bidders would ease competition for farmland and lower the price barrier to entering or expanding a farm. Cooperatives that meet the bill's farmer-controlled definition are expressly allowed to buy land.

industries.industry: Rural landowners selling to corporate buyers
industries.note: Farm owners planning to sell would lose a pool of wealthy buyers, which could mean somewhat lower sale prices for them even as it lowers prices for the next generation of farmers.

analysis.trajectory: With one independent cosponsor and no Democratic cosponsors in a Republican-controlled Senate, the bill is very likely to remain in the Agriculture Committee without a hearing or vote for the rest of the 119th Congress, as similar corporate-farmland bills have in past sessions.
